topic.subject: science
topic.title: Carbon and its compounds
topic.scope: covalent bonding, versatility of carbon, hydrocarbons, functional groups, ethanol, ethanoic acid, soaps and detergents

misconceptions.statement: Covalent bonds are weaker than ionic bonds because sharing is less permanent than giving.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the social meaning of 'sharing' (temporary) versus 'giving' (permanent) to chemical bonds.
misconceptions.fix: Covalent bonds are strong chemical bonds formed by the mutual sharing of electron pairs between atoms to achieve stability.

probe.question: Which bond is inherently 'weak' because atoms can take back their shared electrons?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Carbon can only form four single bonds.
misconceptions.why: Students interpret 'tetravalency' as exactly four separate lines or connections.
misconceptions.fix: Carbon has four valence electrons and can form four single bonds, or combinations of double and triple bonds to satisfy its valency.

probe.question: Can a carbon atom be part of a triple bond and still follow the tetravalency rule?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it can only have four single bonds.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule has only one visual representation

misconceptions.statement: Saturated hydrocarbons are more reactive because they are 'full' of energy.
misconceptions.why: The word 'saturated' is associated with being full or heavy in everyday contexts like fats or sponges.
misconceptions.fix: Saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes) are generally unreactive because all carbon valencies are satisfied by single bonds.

probe.question: Which is more reactive: an alkane or an alkene?

misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's studies on student ideas

misconceptions.statement: The -OH group in alcohols makes the solution basic like NaOH.
misconceptions.why: Students see 'OH' and immediately associate it with the hydroxide ion (OH-) from inorganic bases.
misconceptions.fix: The -OH in alcohols is a covalently bonded functional group and does not ionize in water to release hydroxide ions.

probe.question: Will ethanol turn red litmus paper blue because of its -OH group?

misconceptions.statement: Members of a homologous series have the same physical properties.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse 'similar chemical properties' with 'identical physical properties'.
misconceptions.fix: Members of a homologous series show a regular gradation in physical properties (like boiling point) as molecular mass increases.

probe.question: Do methane and butane have the same boiling point since they are both alkanes?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they are in the same series.

misconceptions.root_belief: similarity in one aspect means similarity in all

misconceptions.statement: Addition reactions can occur in alkanes if you add enough reagent.
misconceptions.why: Students think 'addition' just means adding any chemical to another.
misconceptions.fix: Addition reactions only occur in unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkenes/alkynes) where a double or triple bond can open up.

probe.question: Can you add hydrogen to ethane to make it more saturated?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: The hydrophobic tail of a soap molecule attracts water.
misconceptions.fix: The hydrophobic tail is 'water-fearing' and dissolves in oils, while the hydrophilic head is 'water-loving'.

probe.question: Which part of the soap molecule points towards the water in a micelle?

misconceptions.statement: Scum is formed because soap evaporates in hard water.
misconceptions.why: Students observe the disappearance of lather and the appearance of a solid, assuming the liquid part 'left'.
misconceptions.fix: Scum is an insoluble precipitate formed when soap reacts with calcium and magnesium salts in hard water.

probe.question: What is the white curd-like substance formed when soap is used in hard water?

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Ethanoic acid is a strong acid because it is used in laboratories.
misconceptions.why: Students often believe all 'chemical' acids are strong, unlike 'natural' ones.
misconceptions.fix: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid because it does not ionize completely in water, unlike mineral acids like HCl.

probe.question: Is vinegar (dilute ethanoic acid) a strong acid?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a pure chemical.

misconceptions.root_belief: chemicals are inherently powerful or dangerous

misconceptions.statement: In a dot structure, the shared electrons belong only to the atom that originally brought them.
misconceptions.why: Students struggle with the concept of 'collective ownership' of electrons in a bond.
misconceptions.fix: Shared electrons in a covalent bond belong to the valence shells of both participating atoms simultaneously.

probe.question: In H-H, does each electron still only belong to its original hydrogen atom?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they just sit next to each other.

misconceptions.root_belief: objects retain their original identity in a group

misconceptions.statement: Catenation is unique to carbon and no other element can do it.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks emphasize carbon's catenation so much that students assume it is an exclusive property.
misconceptions.fix: While carbon shows catenation to the maximum extent, other elements like Silicon also show catenation, though to a much lesser degree.

probe.question: Can any element other than carbon form chains of its own atoms?

misconceptions.root_belief: a highlighted property is an exclusive property

misconceptions.statement: Micelles are flat circles of soap molecules on the surface of water.
misconceptions.why: Textbook diagrams are 2D, leading students to perceive 3D structures as flat shapes.
misconceptions.fix: Micelles are spherical clusters where the hydrophobic tails point inwards and hydrophilic heads point outwards in 3D space.

probe.question: What is the 3D shape of a soap micelle in water?
